assumptions: Customer funds remain entirely with an authorized payment or escrow provider and the venture does not inadvertently perform a regulated custody activity.
One renovation milestone can be defined objectively enough for owners, contractors, assessors, and funders to accept the same evidence standard.
Qualified assessors are available at a cost compatible with the proposed fee.
The initial pilot is restricted to a narrow project type rather than the full marketplace vision.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A quantified dispute-loss study, a paid anchor pilot, signed willingness from every required counterparty, a specialist opinion on payment and professional-regulation boundaries, and completed-project data on assessor cost, exception rate, release time, and contribution margin are needed.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Binding a pre-agreed milestone, independent evidence, assessor identity, counterparty sign-off, and a regulated payment instruction addresses a real coordination failure rather than merely digitizing a checklist. The insight is coherent, but it remains a future-state design without demonstrated adoption.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Ambiguous completion can cause rework, delays, and disputes, giving the mechanism plausible value on sufficiently large staged projects. The packet does not quantify dispute frequency or cost, identify a consistently motivated payer, or show willingness to pay the proposed assessment fee or take rate.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: A fee at each accepted milestone could create repeated revenue within a project, and keeping client money with an authorized provider is structurally sound. However, assessor payouts, payment fees, integration, professional liability, security, and dispute administration make the unvalidated 30-50% margin fragile, especially at 800-2,500 PLN per assessment.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Renovation activity and staged finance provide a broad potential market, but small commercial and multi-family projects are still too heterogeneous for a crisp first beachhead. No Polish lender, energy-service firm, contractor network, owner segment, or repeatable milestone type has been selected and validated.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Neutrality and portable acceptance records could differentiate the exchange, but lenders, construction-management platforms, payment providers, and energy-service companies already control adjacent workflows and can bundle the feature. The venture currently controls none of the required transaction participants.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: If accepted as a transaction rail, the model could expand across renovation categories, multiple milestones, portfolios, finance partners, assessors, and jurisdictions. This upside depends on first solving a difficult multi-party standardization and trust problem.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: A trusted network plus proprietary evidence, rejection, remediation, and outcome histories could reduce assessment cost and create switching friction. Those assets do not yet exist, agreements would be nonexclusive, and an incumbent transaction owner could reproduce the workflow.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: The founder's analysis skills and renewable familiarity help define acceptance logic, but there is no current relationship or proprietary asset spanning owners, contractors, assessors, financiers, and payment providers. The claimed control point is entirely dependent on future agreements.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: European renovation-passport policy and electronic trust infrastructure support more structured renovation records and digital sign-off. These policies do not establish demand for the exchange itself, and the thesis anticipates a 2032 norm that may take years to materialize.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Embedding in loan, passport, tender, or energy-service workflows reaches buyers at the correct moment. Each route requires slow institutional or multi-party sales, no partner is committed, and the relationship initially belongs to the lender, contractor, adviser, or energy-service company.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: A no-funds-held evidence pilot may fit the capital limit, but the full model coordinates five stakeholder types, qualified field labor, acceptance standards, regulated payment routing, cyber controls, liability, and disputes. This is a high-complexity operating and legal system for a part-time founder.

highest_value_structural_change: Begin as a fixed-price acceptance service for one repeatable, high-value renovation milestone sponsored by a single lender or energy-service company, with preapproved assessors and no payment routing; add the transaction rail only after acceptance and dispute data prove the standard.
main_structural_strength: The design places the product directly at the fund-release decision and could make acceptance evidence, assessor accountability, and payment progression one coherent transaction rather than disconnected services.
primary_score_limiter: The venture must win coordinated adoption from owners, contractors, assessors, financiers, and a regulated payment provider despite having no current agreement, validated payer, or standardized starting milestone.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Small projects may continue to rely on direct invoices and trust, while lenders and construction platforms can already provide sufficient milestone control and bundle any missing evidence feature into their owned workflow.
